title: Multiple Radius Map: Rings Around a Point
description: Draw several radius rings around one centre on the Multiple Radius Map — 5, 10 and 25-mile circles compared area by area. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, rings of 5, 10 and 25 miles around one centre enclose 78.5, 314.2 and 1,963.5 square miles — the outer ring holds twenty-five times the inner one's ground.
quick_answer: The Multiple Radius Map draws several concentric radius circles around a single centre point, so distances compare in bands — who falls within 5 miles, what 10 adds, how far 25 reaches. Set the centre, add your radii and read the map — delivery zones and catchments in one picture.

body.t: Doubling the radius quadruples the area: 5 mi → 78.5 sq mi; 10 mi → 314.2. The 10–25 ring alone (1,649.3 sq mi) holds more than five times the entire 10-mile circle — outer rings are vaster than they look, which is the map's standing lesson.
Two 10-mile circles whose centres stand 10 miles apart overlap by 39.1% of each circle — the geometry behind duplicate-coverage audits when two branches' rings are drawn together.

faq: How many rings can I draw?

As many as the comparison needs — three to five bands is the readable range; beyond that the map becomes a target and the story blurs. Choose radii that match decisions (fees, times, policies), not round numbers alone.
Both — rings accept either unit, and mixed-unit comparisons (a 5-mile and a 10-km ring) draw faithfully side by side.
Is the area inside a ring the service area?
Geographically yes, operationally not quite: roads, rivers and one-way systems make real reach irregular. Rings are the honest first draft; drive-time tools draw the working version.
Any address or coordinate can anchor the rings — a depot, a store, a competitor. The geometry does not care whose centre it is.
Two centres' rings on one map?
Comparing two locations' bands is the classic site-selection sketch — draw each centre in turn, or use the store catchment tools for the formal version.
Ring maps screenshot and share like any map view; where the tool offers export or share links, the radii travel with the centre so the picture is reproducible.
Why do outer rings look thin but hold so much?
Because area grows with radius squared while the ring's width on screen grows linearly — the map's most reliable optical illusion, and the reason this page tabulates areas beside the picture.
That is a data join, not geometry: the Population Within Radius tool counts people per circle, and repeating it per radius builds the band table.
